chapters.subjectPath: 101 ISK > Anatomy > General Embryology > Fetal Membranes
keyPoints: Fetal membranes are the tissues that protect, support and provide the embryo with nutrition: chorion and chorionic villi, placenta, amnion, umbilical cord and yolk sac.

The placenta is a temporary organ developing in the uterus during pregnancy, the vital connection between mother and developing fetus; it is disc-shaped and lies mostly in the upper segment of the posterior wall of the uterine cavity near the fundus.

The fetal surface is smooth, covered with transparent amnion, with the umbilical cord attached near its centre and umbilical vessels running on it to reach the tertiary villi; the maternal surface is fixed to the uterine wall, shows cotyledons separated by grooves, and is covered by a thin layer of decidua basalis.
The placenta is formed by union of a maternal part - the decidual plate (decidua basalis) - and a fetal part - the chorionic plate (chorion frondosum).

The chorionic plate is formed, from outside the placenta inwards, of amnion, somatopleuric extra-embryonic mesoderm, cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, and carries the umbilical vessels entering (arteries) and leaving (veins) the villi.

The decidual plate is formed, from outside inwards, of decidua basalis containing maternal arterioles, venules and uterine glands, the cytotrophoblastic shell, and syncytiotrophoblast lining the intervillous spaces.

Each tertiary villus is composed, from its outer layer to its core, of syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, somatic mesoderm and endothelium of fetal blood vessels; each has a stem (anchoring) part and absorbing (free or floating) parts.
Intervillous spaces are intercommunicating spaces between tertiary villi receiving their floating branches, containing maternal blood derived from uterine arterioles of the decidua basalis.

Placental (decidual) septa are incomplete septa extending from the decidual plate into the intervillous spaces, each with a core of decidua basalis covered by cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast; opposite each septum is a groove on the maternal surface separating the cotyledons.
Maternal placental circulation: arterial blood flows to the intervillous spaces through decidual arterioles and, after exchange, flows back to the decidual venules.

Fetal placental circulation: umbilical arteries carry fetal blood from fetus to placenta through the umbilical cord and run on the fetal surface to enter the tertiary villi; after exchange, fetal blood is drained through an umbilical vein back to the fetus.

The placental barrier separates maternal blood in the intervillous spaces from fetal blood in the tertiary villi. In early pregnancy it is syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, somatic mesoderm and fetal vessel endothelium; in the second half of pregnancy it is only syncytiotrophoblast and fetal vessel endothelium, becoming thinner to allow rapid exchange for the larger fetus.

Placental barrier functions: separates fetal from maternal blood; permits exchange of nutrients, gases and waste products; prevents passage of bacteria and most viruses, with named exceptions; and mostly prevents passage of toxic material and maternal hormones.

Placental functions: exchange of metabolic products; exchange of gases; transmission of maternal antibodies to fetal blood so the fetus gains immunity; endocrine function; protective role; and excretory function removing fetal urea and creatinine.

Placental hormones: progesterone maintains the endometrium of pregnancy; oestrogen stimulates uterine growth and maturation of the mammary gland; human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) maintains the corpus luteum and is used to detect pregnancy; somatomammotropin gives the fetus priority on maternal blood glucose and promotes breast development.

Congenital anomalies of the placenta are grouped by position, shape (bilobed or trilobed), number (twin or accessory placenta), attachment of the umbilical cord (velamentous - cord attached through the amniotic membrane; battledore - cord attached to the margin), diameter (placenta membranacea, thinner and wider) and infiltration (accreta, increta, percreta).

The amnion is the wall of the amniotic cavity; the amniotic cavity appears within the inner cell mass, after which the embryoblast differentiates into amnioblast cells adjacent to cytotrophoblast and epiblast cells adjacent to hypoblast, the amnio-ectodermal junction being where amnion meets the periphery of the ectoderm.

Expansion of the amniotic cavity causes folding of the embryonic disc with formation of the primitive umbilical ring, forms a sheath of amnion around the umbilical cord, covers the fetal surface of the placenta, brings amnion into contact with chorion forming the amniochorionic membrane with obliteration of the chorionic cavity, and finally brings that membrane with decidua capsularis into contact with decidua parietalis, obliterating the uterine cavity.

Amniotic fluid is a clear watery fluid of water, electrolytes, protein, carbohydrates, lipids, phospholipids and urea; it is first produced by amnioblast cells, then derived from maternal blood by osmosis, and fetal urine is added after kidney development.

Functions of amniotic fluid in early pregnancy: shock absorber protecting the fetus from external trauma, thermal insulator ensuring constant fetal temperature, prevention of adhesion of the fetus to the uterine wall and of fetal body parts to each other.

Functions in late pregnancy: space for fetal movements essential for development of fetal muscles, space for accumulation of fetal urine, and a medium the fetus starts to swallow to learn how to suckle.

Functions during delivery: protects the fetus against uterine contractions, the fore bag of the amniotic sac helps gradual dilatation of the cervical canal, rupture of the amniotic sac is the sign of the start of labour, and sterile amniotic fluid washes the vagina just before passage of the fetus.
The book states that amniotic fluid contains considerable amounts of stem cells and is a source of stem cells.

Polyhydramnios is increased amniotic fluid at full term, with causes including unknown cause in a third of cases, maternal diabetes, congenital malformation of the oesophagus (e.g. oesophageal atresia) interfering with fetal swallowing, and CNS malformation such as anencephaly.
Oligohydramnios is decreased amniotic fluid at full term and may result from bilateral renal agenesis or obstruction of the urinary tract.

The umbilical cord connects the fetus with the placenta, extending between the fetal surface of the placenta and the ventral aspect of the fetal abdominal wall; it is tortuous because of the wavy course of the umbilical arteries, and a wider curve of an umbilical artery may form a false knot with no fetal stress.

The cord contains two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein embedded in Wharton's jelly and ensheathed with amnion; it transmits fetal blood between fetus and placenta and allows free mobility of the fetus.

Development of the cord: the primitive umbilical ring forms during the 4th week as the expanding amniotic cavity folds the disc and shifts the amnio-ectodermal junction ventrally; its contents are the allantois and umbilical vessels inside the connecting stalk and the vitelline duct with vitelline vessels.

The primitive umbilical cord forms when amnion ensheathes the structures passing through the ring; its contents are the secondary yolk sac, vitelline duct and vessels, the connecting stalk, remnant of allantois and umbilical vessels, and later the herniated intestinal loops (physiological umbilical hernia).

The definitive umbilical cord forms when the intestinal loop returns to the abdominal cavity, one umbilical vein and the extra-embryonic part of the vitelline vessels obliterate, the vitelline duct, secondary yolk sac and extra-embryonic allantois degenerate, and Wharton's jelly forms from the mesoderm of the connecting stalk.

Congenital anomalies of the cord: short cord limiting fetal movement and causing premature separation of placenta during delivery; long cord which may encircle the fetal neck or form a true knot; congenital umbilical hernia (omphalocele) from failure of return of the intestine; presence of one umbilical artery from degeneration of the other; and abnormal attachment to the placenta (battledore, or ending outside the placenta with vessels running through the amnion).

The primary yolk sac forms when flat cells derived from hypoblast form Heuser's membrane lining the blastocele; the secondary (definitive) yolk sac forms by new hypoblast-derived cells lining Heuser's membrane, size reduction by pinching off from the growing chorionic cavity, and formation of the allantois as a diverticulum from its caudal wall into the connecting stalk.

After folding, the secondary yolk sac is compressed to form the vitelline (vitello-intestinal) duct connecting the midgut with the part of the yolk sac outside the folded disc; the secondary yolk sac and vitelline duct are gradually reduced and finally degenerate.

Functions of the yolk sac: shares with endoderm in formation of the gut; forms the apex of the urinary bladder from the proximal part of the allantois; primordial germ cells develop when epiblast migrates to the wall of its caudal part; blood vessels of the gut develop in the mesoderm around the vitelline duct, the intra-embryonic part forming gut blood supply while the extra-embryonic part disappears; and blood cells develop in its splanchnic extra-embryonic mesoderm in early pregnancy.

keyPoints: The fetal period is the period from the beginning of the 9th week till birth.
It is characterised by maturation of tissues and organs as well as rapid growth of the body.

Fetal length is indicated as crown-rump length (CRL, sitting height) or crown-heel length (CHL, from the vertex of the skull to the heel, standing height); these measurements are correlated with the age of the fetus in weeks in a table.
Relative size of head to body changes across gestation, from a large fraction of crown-rump length early to a smaller fraction of crown-heel length at birth.
Changes in external features: the face becomes human-looking and the limbs become longer during the 3rd month; external genitalia are differentiated at the end of the 3rd month.
Lanugo hair covers the fetus starting from the 4th month, and the skin is covered by a fatty substance called vernix caseosa at the 5th month.
The skin remains wrinkled till the end of the 6th month because of the absence of subcutaneous fat.
The testes descend to the scrotum just before birth.
Fetal movements are clearly recognised from the fifth month of pregnancy.
Duration of pregnancy is counted either from the first day of the last menstruation or, more accurately, from fertilisation.

keyPoints: The anatomical erect position is used as the reference for describing the anatomy of the body: standing erect, eyes looking forwards, upper limbs hanging by the sides, palms facing forwards and thumbs directed laterally.
Supine position: the body lies on its back. Prone position: the body lies on its face.
Lithotomy position: the body lies on its back with flexion of hip and knee and abduction of the hip joints.
Lateral decubitus position: the body lies on its side, right or left.
The median (sagittal) plane is the vertical plane passing in the midline of the body dividing it into equal right and left halves.
The paramedian plane is parallel to and near the median plane.
The coronal (frontal) plane cuts the body vertically into an anterior part towards the front and a posterior part towards the back.
The horizontal (transverse) plane runs horizontally cutting the body into upper (superior) and lower (inferior) parts.

chapters.subjectPath: 101 ISK > Anatomy > Basis of Anatomy > Fascia
keyPoints: Fascia is a collection of connective tissue under the skin covering the body wall and limbs; it includes superficial, deep and internal fasciae.
Superficial fascia is a layer of loose connective tissue just deep to the skin allowing the skin to move more or less freely over underlying structures.
It contains a variable quantity of fat, more in females: abundant in the gluteal region, anterior abdominal wall and breast; less in the limbs; absent in the eyelid, penis and scrotum.

Functions of superficial fascia: prevents heat loss acting as a thermal insulator; softens and smoothens the body surface; facilitates movement of the skin over underlying structures; acts as the medium conducting nerves, vessels and lymphatics to the skin; contains skin muscles as in the face (muscles of expression); and contains special glands such as the mammary glands.

Deep fascia is a non-elastic membrane of compact regular collagen fibres, well defined in the limbs, very strong and thick in palm and sole, and absent in the face and in the anterior wall of the abdomen.
Deep fascia forms broad sheets around groups of body muscles to give muscle attachment, fix underlying structures in position and help venous return.
Deep fascia forms intermuscular septa and interosseous membranes separating muscle groups of different action and nerve supply, and increasing surface area for muscle attachment.
Deep fascia forms retinacula - localised transverse thickened bands around wrist and ankle joints keeping the tendons in position.
Deep fascia forms the palmar aponeurosis in the palm and the plantar aponeurosis in the sole, very thick strong layers protecting the underlying vessels, nerves and tendons.
Deep fascia forms fibrous sheaths around big vessels, e.g. the carotid sheath in the neck around the common carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus.

chapters.subjectPath: 101 ISK > Anatomy > Basis of Anatomy > Skeletal system
keyPoints: Bone is a hard type of connective tissue which forms the skeleton.

Functions of the skeleton: gives the specific shape to the body; provides the central axis and the skeleton of both limbs; protects vital organs (skull protects the brain, thoracic cage the heart and lungs); provides surface area for muscular attachment; transmits and supports body weight; forms the joints as part of the locomotor system; forms the blood elements in the bone marrow; and stores calcium salts.
By position, the skeleton is axial (skull, mandible, hyoid, sternum, ribs and vertebral column) or appendicular/peripheral (in the upper and lower limbs).

By ossification, bones form by intra-membranous ossification (e.g. clavicle and skull cap - bone develops directly from CT membrane/mesenchyme beginning at one or more centres) or intra-cartilaginous ossification (e.g. long bones, vertebrae, ribs and base of skull - mesenchyme first becomes a cartilage model which is then changed into bone).
By shape there are six classes: long, short, flat, pneumatic, irregular and sesamoid bones.
A long bone has two ends (epiphyses) and a shaft (diaphysis); the epiphysis is the expanded end used for articulation and covered with hyaline cartilage.

The diaphysis is a tube of compact bone with a central medullary cavity lined with endosteum and filled with bone marrow, covered by a fibrous sheath, the periosteum; in growing long bones the epiphysis and diaphysis are separated by a disc of hyaline cartilage, the epiphyseal cartilage.
The metaphysis lies just beneath the epiphyseal cartilage and is the most active part of the long bone.
Short bones (carpal and tarsal bones) consist of spongy bone covered with a thin layer of compact bone.

Flat bones (skull cap, scapula, ribs) consist of two thin plates of compact bone with a middle layer of spongy bone; in skull bones the compact plates are the outer and inner tables and the intervening spongy layer is the diploe.

Pneumatic bones contain air, mainly skull bones surrounding the nose (maxillary, frontal), so the air cavities are called paranasal sinuses; a bone may contain one air cavity (maxillary sinus) or multiple small air cells (mastoid air cells). They decrease the weight of the skull, give resonance of voice and have highly vascular mucosa to warm inspired air.
Irregular bones have irregular shape with projecting processes, e.g. vertebrae, and are similar in structure to short bones.

Sesamoid bones are small nodules of bone embedded in some muscle tendons, e.g. the patella - the largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the tendon of quadriceps femoris in front of the knee joint - and they diminish friction between tendons and underlying bones.

Long bones increase in length from the epiphysial plates of cartilage by proliferation of their cells; the epiphyseal plate at one end ossifies earlier than the other, and the later-ossifying end is called the growing end. Fusion of epiphysis and diaphysis is under hormonal control and occurs earlier in females.
Long bones increase in width from the osteoblasts present in the inner layer of the periosteum.

Arterial supply of bone: the nutrient artery enters the middle of the shaft through an oblique nutrient foramen and runs away from the growing end, supplying the inner two-thirds of the shaft; metaphyseal arteries enter through minute foramina to supply the metaphyses; epiphyseal arteries supply the epiphysis and anastomose with metaphyseal arteries after ossification of the epiphyseal plate; periosteal arteries supply the outer third of the shaft.

Terms of bony elevation are defined: process (elongated projection with a blunt end), spine (elongated with a pointed tip), tubercle/tuberosity/trochanter (localised roughly rounded elevations, smallest to biggest), epicondyle (small elevation above a condyle or articular surface), hamulus (slender curved hook-like process), cornu (slender curved horn-like process), crest (elongated ridge on top of a bone), ridge (linear elevation), line (slightly elevated or rough linear landmark) and condyle (knuckle-shaped structure).

Terms of bony depression are defined: fossa (depression on a surface; a fovea is a small fossa), notch (limited depression with two limiting edges), incisura (cut or notch-like depression on a border), groove or sulcus (elongated depression), fissure (long cleft between flat bones), hiatus (gap or cleft), foramen (hole through a bone), aperture (large hole), canal (track of some length with open ends), meatus (bony canal with one closed end) and impression (slight indentation).

Sex differences in bones: male bones are heavy and thick while female bones are light and thin; tubercles, tuberosities and ridges are more prominent in male bones; and the cavity of the pelvis is wider and shorter in the female to adapt to pregnancy and delivery.

Cartilage is a rubbery type of connective tissue, tough and resilient, with no blood vessels, nerves or lymphatics; it gets nutrition by diffusion from the blood vessels of the perichondrium, consists of mature cartilage cells (chondrocytes), fibres and matrix, resists compression forces and friction, and has great capacity of growth by multiplication of chondroblasts.

Hyaline cartilage (glass-like) is the most widespread in the human body, with translucent matrix and numerous small rounded cartilage cells; it is found in developing bones in the fetus, epiphyseal plates of long bones, articular cartilage in joints, costal cartilage and xiphoid process, and the larynx (except the epiglottis) and tracheal rings. It ossifies in old age in certain sites such as the larynx and epiphyseal cartilages.
White fibrocartilage has an opaque matrix rich in collagen bundles and few cartilage cells; it is found in the intervertebral discs and does not ossify in old age.

Yellow elastic fibrocartilage has a yellow matrix rich in yellow elastic fibres and abundant cartilage cells; it is found in the tip of the nose, auricle of the ear and epiglottis of the larynx, and does not ossify in old age.

chapters.subjectPath: 101 ISK > Anatomy > Basis of Anatomy > Articular system
keyPoints: A joint is the contact between two bones or more.
Joints are classified into fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial.
Fibrous joints are fixed or immobile, the bone surfaces being connected by fibrous tissue; there are three types - syndesmosis, gomphosis and sutures.
Syndesmosis is present in the inferior tibio-fibular joint where the lower ends of tibia and fibula are connected by fibrous tissue called the interosseous ligament.
Gomphosis is present in the teeth, where the roots are connected to their sockets in the mandible and maxilla by fibrous tissue called the periodontal ligament.
Sutures are present in the skull, where the bones are connected by a thin layer of fibrous tissue called the sutural ligament; they are obliterated in old age.

Primary cartilaginous joints are temporary and disappear by ossification; they lie at the ends of long bones, are immobile, and are a plate of hyaline cartilage between epiphysis and diaphysis in developing long bones in children.

Secondary cartilaginous joints are permanent, present in the midline (e.g. intervertebral discs), with limited mobility facilitated by the elasticity of the fibrocartilaginous disc; the articulating bone is covered by a thin layer of hyaline cartilage and separated by a white fibrocartilaginous disc, strengthened by fibrous ligaments which do not form a complete capsule.

A synovial joint is freely mobile, present mostly in the limbs, and is formed of fibrous capsule, articular cartilage, joint cavity, synovial membrane, synovial fluid, ligaments and intra-articular structures.
The fibrous capsule surrounds the joint, is lined by synovial membrane and is supported and strengthened by strong ligaments.

Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage covering the articular surfaces; it is smooth and lubricated by synovial fluid, has no blood vessels or nerves, is nourished from synovial fluid, and in old age shows irregularities and undulations due to erosions which do not repair.
The joint cavity is a potential cavity containing a very thin film of synovial fluid; it becomes manifest if fluid, blood or pus collects in it.

The synovial membrane is a thin, moist, glistening membrane covering all structures inside the joint except the articular surfaces; it lines the fibrous capsule and secretes and absorbs the synovial fluid.

Synovial fluid is a pale yellow viscous fluid similar to egg albumin containing free cells (synovial cells, macrophages and lymphocytes); it lubricates the articular cartilage and reduces its erosion and helps its nutrition.
Ligaments support and strengthen the joint and include capsular, extracapsular and intracapsular ligaments.

Intra-articular structures include an articular fibrocartilaginous disc dividing the cavity into upper and lower compartments (temporomandibular joint), menisci or semilunar cartilages (knee joint), ligaments (cruciate ligament of the knee) and tendons (tendon of the long head of biceps in the shoulder joint).

Factors affecting the stability of the joint: shape and fitting of articulating surfaces, thickness and elasticity of the capsule, position and strength of ligaments, and strength of the muscles surrounding the joint.
Factors affecting the range of movement: tension of ligaments surrounding the joint, contraction of the antagonistic muscles, and approximation and contact of the soft tissues around the joint.
The sensory nerves supplying a joint are called articular nerves; they end in the fibrous capsule and related ligaments and are sensitive to pain, position and movement of the joint.
Hilton's Law: the nerve supply to a muscle acting on a specific joint gives a branch to supply this joint and another branch to supply the skin covering the same joint.

Joint movements defined: flexion (approximation of two ventral aspects), extension (straightening), abduction (movement away from the midline - in fingers away from the middle finger, in toes away from the second toe), adduction (movement towards the midline), circumduction (combination of all the above), rotation (medial or lateral rotation of the limb around a vertical axis), gliding (non-axial movement), supination (lateral rotation of the forearm), pronation (medial rotation of the forearm), inversion (sole directed inwards), eversion (sole directed outwards) and opposition (thumb coming into contact with the other four fingers).
By number of articulating bones synovial joints are simple (two bones, e.g. shoulder), compound (more than two bones, e.g. elbow) or complex (containing intra-articular structures, e.g. knee).

Uni-axial joints move around a single axis: a hinge joint has a trochlea-like convex articular surface and one transverse axis, allowing only flexion and extension because of strong collateral ligaments (elbow); a pivot joint has a central bony pivot surrounded by a fibro-osseous ring and allows rotation around a longitudinal axis (superior radio-ulnar joint).

Bi-axial joints move around two perpendicular axes and are condylar (two convex condyles articulating with two concave surfaces - knee, bicondylar; or one condyle with one concave surface - temporomandibular joint, unicondylar), ellipsoid (an oval convex surface of the carpal bones with the elliptical concave inferior surface of radius and the articular disc of ulna - wrist joint) or saddle (concavo-convex articulating surfaces - carpometacarpal joint of the thumb).

Multi-axial joints move around three axes; a globular rounded bone articulates with a concave socket, making them the most freely mobile joints in the body - the ball and socket joints of shoulder and hip.
Non-axial (plane) joints have flat articular surfaces and gliding movement without any axis, e.g. intercarpal joints, superior tibio-fibular joint and intervertebral joints.

chapters.subjectPath: 101 ISK > Anatomy > Basis of Anatomy > Muscular system
keyPoints: Muscle tissue is characterised by the property of contraction - the ability of the muscle fibres to become short.
By structure and function there are three types of muscle: skeletal, smooth and cardiac.
Skeletal muscle is attached to the skeleton, contracts voluntarily, is striated and is supplied by somatic nerves.
Smooth muscle is in the wall of blood vessels and viscera, contracts involuntarily, has no striations and is supplied by autonomic nerves.
Cardiac muscle is in the myocardium of the heart, contracts involuntarily, is striated but less than skeletal muscle, and is supplied by autonomic nerves.

Each skeletal muscle has two attachments: the origin is the most fixed attachment and the insertion the most mobile; sometimes the insertion is the fixed point and the origin mobile, and a muscle may have more than one origin or insertion.
In the limbs the origins are usually proximal to the insertions, and during contraction the insertion moves towards the origin, producing movement in the related joints.

Types of muscle attachment: to bone (commonest, either directly by fleshy fibres or by a tendon); to a fibrous raphe (a band or septum of fibrous tissue through which two muscles fuse, e.g. mylohyoid); to skin (inserted into the dermis so contraction moves the skin, e.g. facial muscles); and to cartilage (e.g. cricothyroid muscle of the larynx).

Skeletal muscles vary in shape and fibre arrangement to produce a specific force and range of contraction; the form depends on the arrangement of fibres relative to the line of pull, the line extending between origin and insertion.
Muscles with fibres parallel to the line of pull: strap-like (sartorius), strap-like with tendinous intersections (rectus abdominis), quadrilateral (thyrohyoid) and fusiform (lumbrical).

Pennate (feather-like) muscles have fibres oblique to the tendons and are unipennate (fibres on one side of the tendon, flexor pollicis longus), bipennate (fibres on both sides, rectus femoris), multipennate (a series of bipennate units side by side, deltoid) and circumpennate (cylindrical with a central tendon and bipennate units converging from the periphery, tibialis anterior).
Non-pennate oblique muscles are triangular (temporalis), spiral (supinator), cruciate (masseter) and circular (orbicularis oris).
Muscles may have more than one fleshy belly or head: two heads (biceps), three heads (triceps) or four heads (quadriceps).
A purposeful movement is not done by one muscle but by a group acting together; by role there are four types of muscle action.

Prime mover (agonist) initiates and maintains a movement; antagonist opposes the action of the prime mover; fixator (stabiliser) fixes the origin of the prime mover or stabilises the joint on which it acts; synergist contracts to eliminate unwanted movements at joints the prime mover crosses so that its action on the desired joint becomes maximal.

chapters.subjectPath: 101 ISK > Anatomy > Basis of Anatomy > Nervous system
keyPoints: The nervous system is classified into central (brain inside the skull, and spinal cord) and peripheral (nerves - spinal and cranial - and the autonomic nervous system, sympathetic and parasympathetic).

Parts of the brain: two cerebral hemispheres (cerebrum) formed of four main lobes - frontal, parietal, occipital and temporal; the cerebellum; the brain stem formed of midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata; and the diencephalon divided into thalamus, subthalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus and metathalamus.
The spinal cord is a tube present inside the vertebral column, with two enlargements, one cervical and one lumbar, where the nerve plexuses arise, and a tapering end called the conus medullaris.
The spinal cord has outer white matter of nerve fibres containing the nervous tracts, inner H-shaped grey matter of nerve cells, and a central canal.

The grey matter forms two dorsal horns containing sensory nuclei, two ventral horns containing motor nuclei, and two lateral horns containing sympathetic nuclei in the thoracic and upper two lumbar segments and parasympathetic nuclei in the 2nd, 3rd and 4th sacral segments.
Each spinal nerve arises from the spinal cord by two roots: an anterior (ventral) root containing motor fibres and a posterior (dorsal) root containing sensory fibres.
The two roots unite to form the nerve trunk containing mixed fibres, which divides into anterior (ventral) and posterior (dorsal) primary rami, both containing mixed fibres.

The cranial nerves arise from the brain and leave the skull through foramina; they are named in order: olfactory, optic, oculomotor, trochlear, trigeminal, abducent, facial, auditory, glossopharyngeal, vagus, accessory and hypoglossal.
The meninges are the coverings of the central nervous system, arranged from inside out as pia mater, arachnoid mater and dura mater.
The autonomic nervous system is concerned with involuntary activities and is divided into sympathetic and parasympathetic parts.

chapters.subjectPath: 101 ISK > Anatomy > Basis of Anatomy > Cardiovascular system
keyPoints: The cardiovascular system consists of the heart and blood vessels.
The heart lies behind the sternum and costal cartilages; about two-thirds lies to the left and one-third to the right of the median plane.
The heart has four chambers: two atria and two ventricles.
The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from all parts of the body by the superior and inferior venae cavae and sends it to the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve.
The right ventricle sends deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary valve to the pulmonary trunk which divides into right and left pulmonary arteries, one for each lung where oxygenation occurs.
The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from both lungs through four pulmonary veins and pumps it to the left ventricle via the mitral valve.
The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to all parts of the body through the aortic valve into the aorta and its branches.
The right half of the heart contains deoxygenated (venous) blood and the left half oxygenated (arterial) blood; the heart is covered by two types of pericardial sac, fibrous and serous pericardium.

Systemic circulation: oxygenated blood from the left ventricle passes through the aorta and its branches to all tissues where exchange of gases and materials occurs; deoxygenated blood is collected by small then large veins and finally the venae cavae into the right atrium and then the right ventricle.

Pulmonary circulation: deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle passes through the pulmonary artery and its two branches to both lungs where gas exchange occurs; oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium via the four pulmonary veins and then to the left ventricle.

Portal circulation: venous blood from stomach, spleen, pancreas and intestine is collected into the portal vein which enters the liver through the porta hepatis and divides into branches ending in liver sinusoids; blood leaves by the hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava. It transmits venous blood from the GIT to the liver to metabolise undigested nutrients and detoxify the blood.

Arteries carry blood from the heart to other regions of the body; they carry oxygenated blood except the pulmonary and umbilical arteries which carry deoxygenated blood, and are classified by size and structure into large, medium-sized and small arteries.

Arterial anastomosis is the connection between arteries, present mainly around the joints; it increases blood supply to some organs, equalises pressure in the communicating arteries, and maintains blood flow to a part if its main artery is obstructed.

End to end anastomosis connects the two ends of two arteries forming an arch, e.g. in the hand and foot, between gastric arteries, between arteries of the gut and between anterior and posterior intercostal arteries.

Anastomosis by terminal arterioles lies around the joints between branches of the main artery above and below the joint; in gradual obstruction it opens to maintain blood supply below the obstruction, e.g. around the elbow joint.
Anastomosis by conversion occurs when two arteries converge to unite together, e.g. between the two vertebral arteries.

End arteries do not anastomose with adjacent arteries, so their obstruction leads to death (necrosis) of the tissues they supply: central retinal artery, renal artery, splenic artery, central branches of cerebral arteries and pulmonary arteries.
Venous return from the upper part of the body is drained mainly by gravity.

Venous return from the lower limb is helped by venous valves, arterial pulsations, muscular contractions (muscle pump), the deep fascia surrounding the muscle groups, and negative intrathoracic pressure drawing blood from abdomen, head and neck into the thorax; from abdomen, pelvis and thorax venous return is by the suction mechanism of negative intrathoracic pressure.

Arteries and veins are connected by capillaries (narrow uniform diameter), sinusoids (wide irregular diameter with dilatations and constrictions) or arteriovenous shunts (between small arteries and accompanying veins).

Arteriovenous shunts are found in the external ear, nail bed and palmar aspects of digits, tongue, thyroid gland, penis and alimentary tract; they are straight or coiled, surrounded by a thick muscular coat and supplied by sympathetic fibres controlling their opening and closure.
Arteriovenous shunts regulate body temperature and local heat (when open, blood passes from artery to vein decreasing local heat), regulate food absorption and play a role in erection.

chapters.subjectPath: 101 ISK > Anatomy > Basis of Anatomy > Lymphatic system
keyPoints: The lymphatic system is responsible for the circulation of the lymph - a clear colourless fluid rich in protein - from the tissue spaces (intercellular spaces) to the blood stream.
It consists of three parts: lymph vessels; lymphoid tissues such as lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils and thymus; and free cells (lymphocytes), including B and T lymphocytes.
Lymph vessels are fine vessels in the tissue spaces uniting into larger vessels which join the lymph nodes; they are of two types.
Afferent lymph vessels open into the periphery of the lymph nodes at their convex borders and carry lymph to them; efferent lymph vessels emerge from the hilum and carry lymph away.
All lymph vessels are collected into two large lymph ducts in the root of the neck which open into two large veins there.

The thoracic duct drains the left side of head and neck, the left upper limb, the left half of the thorax and the whole body below the diaphragm; the right lymphatic duct drains the right side of head and neck, the right half of the thorax and the right upper limb.

Characters of lymph vessels: they begin blindly in the tissue spaces; their walls contain wide pores allowing the passage of fat and proteins; they have many valves making lymph flow in one direction; and they are absent in brain and spinal cord, bone marrow and avascular structures such as cartilage, cornea and hair.
Factors helping the flow and movement of lymph: arterial pulsations, muscular contractions, intrathoracic negative pressure and peristaltic movement of the intestine.

Lymph nodes are oval or kidney-shaped small bodies lying along the course of lymph vessels in groups at fixed sites: at the limb roots (axillary for the upper limb, inguinal for the lower limb), in the neck on both sides and at its junction with the head, in the chest close to trachea and bronchi and in the chest wall, close to the abdominal and pelvic organs near the big vessels, and around the abdominal aorta and the blood vessels of the pelvis.

Functions of lymph nodes: filtration of lymph from bacteria and foreign bodies, formation and production of lymphocytes, and defence - they are the sites of interaction between microorganisms (antigens) and phagocytes and lymphocytes.

The thymus is a lymphatic organ with an endocrine function, secreting thymosin hormone; it is formed of two lobes and lies in the thorax just behind the sternum. It continues to increase in size until puberty and then decreases with advancing age.
The spleen is a haemolymphatic organ in the upper left part of the abdominal cavity beneath the left dome of the diaphragm, behind the stomach and protected by ribs.
The spleen is not palpable unless enlarged at least three times.

Spleen functions: in the fetus it has a role in formation of blood cells; in the adult it stores and concentrates blood cells and, in case of haemorrhage, pours concentrated blood into the circulation; it destroys old expired red cells; and it filters the blood from organisms or harmful substances.
The book emphasises the contrast: the lymph nodes filter the lymph but the spleen filters the blood.

chapters.subjectPath: 101 ISK > Anatomy > Upper Limb > Pectoral Region
keyPoints: The pectoral region is the region on the upper part of the front of the chest wall down to the 6th rib, comprising skin, superficial fascia containing the mammary gland, deep (pectoral) fascia and muscles.

Cutaneous nerves: the supraclavicular nerves (C3,4) - medial, intermediate and lateral - are branches of the cervical plexus supplying the skin between clavicle and 2nd rib including the skin over the upper half of deltoid; the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of intercostal nerves supply the skin below the 2nd rib.
The mammary gland is a modified sweat gland, rudimentary in the male, hemispherical, with a circular base and an axillary tail, and its covering skin carries the nipple and areola.

It lies in the superficial fascia of the pectoral region; its base extends from the 2nd rib above to the 6th costal cartilage below and from the lateral border of the sternum to the mid-axillary line.
The base lies on the deep fascia covering pectoralis major (pectoral fascia) and serratus anterior and on the aponeurosis of the external oblique.

The axillary tail is a tongue-like prolongation from the superolateral quadrant that curves around the lower border of pectoralis major, pierces the deep axillary fascia and extends upwards into the axilla.
Internally the gland consists of lobes embedded in the fat of the superficial fascia arranged radially converging towards the nipple.

Lobes are supported and separated into fascial compartments by fibrous septa called Cooper's ligaments extending from the skin to the deep fascia on the chest wall and suspending the breast to the skin.

Each lobe collects its secretion into a lactiferous duct; all lactiferous ducts converge on the nipple, each widening deep to the areola into a lactiferous sinus then narrowing again to open on the summit of the nipple.
The nipple is a conical projection traversed by the lactiferous ducts; its position changes after the first childbirth and lactation, lying at a variable lower level.

The areola is a circular area of pigmented skin surrounding the base of the nipple; it is pinkish in virgins, becomes darker during the first pregnancy and never returns pinkish again, and contains sebaceous (areolar) glands - Montgomery's tubercles.

Arterial supply of the breast: lateral thoracic artery from the 2nd part of the axillary artery supplying mainly the lateral half; perforating branches of the internal mammary artery supplying mainly the medial half; the pectoral branch of the acromio-thoracic artery from the 2nd part of the axillary artery; and lateral branches of the posterior intercostal arteries as a minimal source.

Breast lymphatics form two plexuses: a superficial (subareolar) plexus under the skin of the areola receiving afferents from the gland and draining through interlobular lymph vessels to the deep plexus, and a deep lymphatic plexus on the deep fascia receiving from the four quadrants and from the superficial plexus and draining along the blood supply.

Lateral quadrants drain mainly to the pectoral group of axillary nodes, the tail to the subscapular group, and the upper lateral part to the infraclavicular nodes (a superficial group lying outside the axilla), whose efferents pierce the anterior wall of the axilla to reach the apical group.

Medial quadrants drain mainly to the parasternal nodes along the internal mammary artery inside the thorax; some lymphatics cross the midline to the deep plexus of the opposite side and some from the lower medial part pierce the abdominal wall to reach the subdiaphragmatic plexus.

The pectoral fascia is the deep fascia of the region covering pectoralis major beneath the breast, with two extensions - the axillary fascia forming the floor of the axilla, and the clavipectoral fascia.

The clavipectoral fascia is a strong fibrous sheet occupying the interval between subclavius above and pectoralis minor below, lying deep to the upper part of pectoralis major and covering the axillary vessels and nerves.

Its attachments: above it splits to enclose subclavius and attaches to the margins of the subclavian groove on the lower surface of the clavicle; medially it is thickened and extends to the 1st and 2nd costal cartilages; laterally it reaches the coracoid process and blends with the coraco-clavicular ligament; below it splits to enclose pectoralis minor, continuing from that muscle's lower border as the suspensory ligament of the axilla to join the axillary fascia.
The fascia from the clavicle to the floor of the axilla is called the axillary septum.

Four structures pierce the clavipectoral fascia: the cephalic vein, the lateral pectoral nerve, the acromio-thoracic artery, and lymph vessels from the infraclavicular nodes draining into the apical group.

Pectoralis major arises by a clavicular head from the anterior surface of the medial half of the clavicle and a sternocostal head from the anterior surface of the sternum, upper costal cartilages and aponeurosis of external abdominal oblique, and inserts by a bilaminar tendon into the lateral lip of the intertubercular (bicipital) groove; it is supplied by the lateral and medial pectoral nerves and adducts and medially rotates the arm, the clavicular head flexing and the sternocostal head extending the flexed arm.

Pectoralis minor arises from the outer surfaces of the 3rd, 4th and 5th ribs near their costal cartilages and inserts into the medial border and upper surface of the coracoid process; supplied by the medial pectoral nerve, it protracts and depresses the shoulder girdle and raises the ribs in forced inspiration when the scapula is fixed.

Subclavius arises from the upper surface of the 1st costo-chondral junction and inserts into a groove on the lower surface of the middle third of the clavicle; supplied by the nerve to subclavius (C5), it steadies the clavicle and prevents excessive shoulder girdle movement.

chapters.bookTitle: MUSCLES CONNECTING THE UPPER LIMB WITH VERTEBRAL COLUMN (Muscles of the Back) (Chapter 2)
keyPoints: The muscles of the back are upper limb muscles situated in the back connecting the limb to the vertebral column; the book states they are supplied by the anterior primary rami of the spinal nerves.
They are arranged in two layers: a superficial layer of trapezius and latissimus dorsi, and a deep layer of levator scapulae, rhomboideus major and rhomboideus minor.

Trapezius arises from the external occipital protuberance and medial third of the superior nuchal line, from the ligamentum nuchae and spine of C7, and from the spines of all thoracic vertebrae and their supraspinous ligaments.

Trapezius has a U-shaped insertion: upper fibres into the posterior border of the lateral third of the clavicle, middle fibres into the medial border of the acromion and the upper lip of the crest of the scapular spine, and lower fibres into a rough tubercle on the crest of the scapular spine near its root.
Trapezius is supplied motor by the spinal root of the accessory nerve and sensory by cervical nerves C3 and C4.

Trapezius actions: upper fibres elevate the shoulder girdle; middle fibres (with the rhomboids) retract the scapula and brace back the shoulder; upper and lower fibres together rotate the scapula so the glenoid cavity faces upward, allowing the arm to be raised overhead.
Latissimus dorsi is a large triangular flat muscle covering the lower half of the back down to the iliac crest, with a wide origin and a narrow tendon of insertion.

It arises by fleshy fibres from the spines of the lower 6 thoracic vertebrae under cover of trapezius, the thoracolumbar fascia, the posterior third of the outer lip of the iliac crest, the outer surface of the lower 4 ribs, and a few fibres from the dorsal aspect of the inferior angle of the scapula.
Latissimus dorsi inserts into the floor of the bicipital groove and is supplied by the thoraco-dorsal nerve (nerve to latissimus dorsi).

Its actions are extension, medial rotation and adduction of the arm; acting with the sternocostal part of pectoralis major it pulls the trunk upwards as in climbing; and through its rib attachment it assists in violent expiration as in coughing.

The upper border of latissimus dorsi crosses over the inferior angle of the scapula and has a triple relation to teres major - first behind it, then curving below it, and at its insertion in front of it.
At its insertion latissimus dorsi usually fuses with teres major forming the posterior axillary fold.

The triangle of auscultation lies medial to the lower part of the scapula, bounded above by the lateral border of trapezius, below by the upper border of latissimus dorsi and laterally by the lower part of the medial border of the scapula; its floor is rhomboideus major and the sixth and seventh ribs with the space between them. Breath sounds are clearly heard over it, hence its name.

The lumbar triangle lies just above the iliac crest, bounded below by the iliac crest, medially by the lateral border of latissimus dorsi and laterally by the posterior border of external abdominal oblique; its floor is internal abdominal oblique and transversus abdominis.

Levator scapulae arises by four slips from the transverse processes of the upper 4 cervical vertebrae and inserts into the dorsal surface of the medial border of the scapula above the root of the spine; it is supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5) plus fibres from C3 and C4, and elevates the shoulder girdle with the upper fibres of trapezius, rotates the scapula so the glenoid cavity faces downward, and retracts the scapula.

Rhomboideus minor arises from the lower part of the ligamentum nuchae and the spines of C7 and T1 and inserts into the dorsal surface of the medial border of the scapula opposite the root of the spine; supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5), it rotates the scapula so the glenoid faces downward (with levator scapulae) and retracts the scapula (with the middle fibres of trapezius).

Rhomboideus major arises from the spines of T2-T5 and their supraspinous ligaments and inserts into the dorsal surface of the medial border of the scapula from the root of the spine to the inferior angle; it is supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5) and has the same actions as rhomboideus minor.

chapters.bookTitle: MUSCLES OF THE SHOULDER REGION (Scapular Muscles) (Chapter 3)
keyPoints: The scapular muscles are a group surrounding the shoulder joint and extending from scapula to humerus: deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres major, teres minor and subscapularis.

Deltoid is a triangular thick muscle forming the rounded contour of the shoulder, with a V-shaped origin from the anterior border of the lateral third of the clavicle (anterior fibres), the lateral border of the acromion (middle fibres) and the lower lip of the crest of the spine of the scapula (posterior fibres).
Deltoid inserts into the deltoid tuberosity at the middle of the lateral surface of the shaft of the humerus and is supplied by the circumflex (axillary) nerve.
Deltoid actions: anterior fibres flex and medially rotate the arm; posterior fibres extend and laterally rotate the arm; middle fibres abduct the arm through the middle range of abduction.

The deltopectoral groove lies between the contiguous borders of pectoralis major and deltoid and ends above, just below the clavicle, in the infraclavicular fossa; it lodges the uppermost part of the cephalic vein, the deltoid branch of the thoraco-acromial artery and the deltopectoral lymph nodes.

Supraspinatus arises from the medial two-thirds of the supraspinous fossa, inserts into the highest impression on the greater tuberosity, is supplied by the suprascapular nerve, helps steady the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity and initiates abduction of the arm.

Infraspinatus arises from the medial two-thirds of the infraspinous fossa, inserts into the middle impression on the back of the greater tuberosity, is supplied by the suprascapular nerve, steadies the head of the humerus and laterally rotates the arm.

Teres minor arises from the upper two-thirds of the dorsal surface of the lateral border of the scapula, inserts into the lowest impression on the back of the greater tuberosity, is supplied by the axillary (circumflex) nerve, steadies the head of the humerus and adducts and laterally rotates the arm.

Teres major arises from the lower third of the dorsal surface of the lateral border of the scapula, inserts into the medial lip of the bicipital groove, is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve, and produces adduction, medial rotation and extension of the arm.

Subscapularis fits the subscapular fossa on the front of the scapula, arising from its medial two-thirds and inserting into the lesser tuberosity of the humerus; it is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves, stabilises the anterior aspect of the shoulder joint and medially rotates and adducts the arm.

Subscapularis together with supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor steady the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity during arm movements; the tendons of these four muscles blend with the capsule of the shoulder joint and are called the rotator muscle cuff.
The muscles connecting the upper limb with the thoracic wall are pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, subclavius and serratus anterior.

Serratus anterior is a large flat muscle covering the upper part of the side of the chest, arising by digitations from the outer surfaces of the upper ribs midway between their angles and their costal cartilages, the first digitation being the largest and arising from the 1st and 2nd ribs.

Serratus anterior inserts into the ventral surface of the medial border of the scapula: the first digitation into the superior angle, the 2nd and 3rd fanning out into the whole length of the medial border, and the lower five converging into the inferior angle.

Serratus anterior is supplied by the nerve to serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve), which arises from the roots of the brachial plexus and descends vertically on the outer surface of the muscle in the mid-axillary line.

Serratus anterior is the main and powerful protractor of the shoulder, assisted by pectoralis minor; acting with the upper and lower fibres of trapezius its lower five digitations rotate the scapula so the glenoid cavity looks upwards; it helps fix the scapula to the chest wall; and when the scapula is fixed it pulls on the ribs in forced inspiration.
The quadrangular and triangular spaces are intermuscular spaces lying just below the shoulder joint.

The quadrangular space (laterally) is bounded above by teres minor (from behind), subscapularis (from in front) and the capsule of the shoulder joint, below by teres major, medially by the long head of triceps and laterally by the surgical neck of the humerus; it contains the posterior circumflex humeral vessels and the axillary (circumflex) nerve.

The upper triangular space (medially) is bounded above by teres minor (from behind) and subscapularis (from in front), below by teres major and laterally by the long head of triceps; it transmits only the circumflex scapular artery.

The lower triangular space (triangular interval) lies just lateral to the long head of triceps, separated from the quadrangular space by teres major; it is bounded above by teres major, medially by the long head of triceps and laterally by the lateral head of triceps and the shaft of the humerus, and contains the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels.

chapters.subjectPath: 101 ISK > Anatomy > Upper Limb > Axilla
keyPoints: The axilla is a pyramidal region situated between the upper part of the side of the chest wall and the upper part of the medial side of the arm; it is a four-sided pyramid with an apex, a base (floor) and four walls - anterior, posterior, lateral and medial.
The apex is the cervico-axillary canal.

The anterior (pectoral) wall has a superficial layer of pectoralis major and a deep layer (axillary septum) of subclavius, clavipectoral fascia, pectoralis minor and the suspensory ligament of the axilla; the lower border of pectoralis major forms the anterior axillary fold and the wall is shorter than the posterior wall.

The posterior (subscapular) wall is formed by the lateral part of subscapularis, teres major and latissimus dorsi; teres major and latissimus dorsi form the posterior axillary fold which lies lower than the anterior fold.
The lateral (humeral) wall is the narrowest and is formed by the bicipital groove of the humerus, the short head of biceps and coracobrachialis.
The medial (costal) wall is formed by the upper four ribs with their intercostal muscles and the upper part of serratus anterior.

The base (floor) looks downwards and is formed by skin rich in hairs, sweat and sebaceous glands, superficial fascia, and deep (axillary) fascia which receives the attachment of the suspensory ligament of the axilla.

Contents of the axilla: the axillary artery and its branches, the axillary vein and its tributaries, the cords of the brachial plexus and their branches, the long thoracic nerve, the intercostobrachial nerve (lateral cutaneous branch of the 2nd thoracic nerve), five groups of axillary lymph nodes, the tail of the mammary gland and axillary fat.
The axillary vessels and brachial plexus run from the apex to the base along the lateral wall of the axilla, nearer to the anterior than the posterior wall.
The brachial plexus lies partly in the neck and partly in the axilla and consists of roots, trunks, divisions and cords.
Roots are formed by the ventral primary rami of the 5th, 6th, 7th and 8th cervical and 1st thoracic nerves.

The upper trunk is formed by union of the 5th and 6th cervical roots, the middle trunk by the 7th cervical root only, and the lower trunk by union of the 8th cervical and 1st thoracic roots; the three trunks lie above the clavicle in the neck.
Each trunk divides behind the clavicle into anterior (ventral) and posterior (dorsal) divisions.

The medial cord is formed by the anterior division of the lower trunk, the lateral cord by fusion of the anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks, and the posterior cord by fusion of the posterior divisions of the three trunks; the cords lie in the axilla.
All branches of the lateral and medial cords supply the flexor side, while all branches of the posterior cord supply the extensor side of the upper limb.

Branches of the roots: the nerve to rhomboids (dorsal scapular nerve), which descends along the medial border of the scapula deep to levator scapulae and the rhomboids and supplies them, and the nerve to serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve).
Branches of the trunks come only from the upper trunk: the nerve to subclavius, which descends in front of the plexus to the muscle, and the suprascapular nerve.

The suprascapular nerve runs downwards and laterally in the neck to the suprascapular notch, passes through the suprascapular foramen below the suprascapular ligament into the supraspinous fossa to supply supraspinatus, then descends through the spinoglenoid notch into the infraspinous fossa to supply infraspinatus, giving articular branches to the acromioclavicular and shoulder joints.

Branches of the lateral cord: musculocutaneous nerve (its largest branch), lateral root of the median nerve, and lateral pectoral nerve which pierces the clavipectoral fascia and supplies pectoralis major.

Branches of the medial cord: ulnar nerve (its largest branch), medial root of the median nerve, medial pectoral nerve which pierces and supplies pectoralis minor and ends by supplying pectoralis major, medial cutaneous nerve of the arm supplying the skin on the medial side of the lower half of the arm, and medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm which descends medial to the third part of the axillary artery and the upper half of the brachial artery to supply the skin of the medial side of the forearm to the wrist.

Branches of the posterior cord: radial nerve (the larger of its two terminal branches), axillary (circumflex) nerve, upper subscapular nerve to the upper part of subscapularis, lower subscapular nerve to the lower part of subscapularis and teres major, and the nerve to latissimus dorsi (thoraco-dorsal nerve).

The axillary nerve passes downwards and laterally, and at the lower border of subscapularis passes backwards through the quadrangular space, winding round the back of the surgical neck of the humerus where it gives an articular branch to the shoulder joint.

The axillary nerve ends as an anterior branch continuing round the surgical neck to end near the anterior border of deltoid and supply it, and a posterior branch giving a branch to teres minor then curving round the posterior border of deltoid as the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm supplying the skin over the lower half of the deltoid.

The axillary artery begins at the outer border of the first rib as the continuation of the subclavian artery, enters the axilla through its apex, runs downwards and laterally along the lateral wall, and ends at the lower border of teres major (lower limit of the axilla) by becoming the brachial artery.
Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts: first part above the muscle, second part deep to it, and third part - the longest - below it.

Relations to the cords: the lateral and posterior cords lie lateral to the first part and the medial cord posterior to it; around the second part the cords lie according to their names - medial, lateral and posterior; and the branches of each cord are distributed around the third part.
The first part of the axillary artery gives the superior thoracic artery, arising at the lower border of subclavius to supply it and anastomose with intercostal arteries.
The second part gives the acromio-thoracic artery and the lateral thoracic artery.

The acromio-thoracic artery is a short trunk arising behind the upper border of pectoralis minor which pierces the clavipectoral fascia and divides into acromial, pectoral (the largest, descending between the two pectoral muscles supplying them and the breast), clavicular (to subclavius and the sternoclavicular joint) and deltoid branches (in the deltopectoral groove to deltoid and pectoralis major).

The lateral thoracic artery arises behind the lower border of pectoralis minor and runs along it to the side of the chest, supplying serratus anterior, the pectoral muscles and subscapularis; in females it is large and gives lateral mammary branches.
The third part gives the subscapular artery (its largest branch), the anterior circumflex humeral artery and the posterior circumflex humeral artery.

The subscapular artery arises at the lower border of subscapularis and gives the circumflex scapular artery, below which it continues as the thoraco-dorsal artery supplying latissimus dorsi and sharing in the anastomosis around the scapula.

The circumflex scapular artery is usually larger than the continuation of the subscapular artery; it curves round the lateral border of the scapula traversing the upper triangular space and shares in the anastomosis around the scapula.

The anterior circumflex humeral artery is very small, arises at the lower border of subscapularis, runs in front of the surgical neck of the humerus, gives an ascending branch to the shoulder joint and anastomoses with the posterior circumflex humeral artery.

The posterior circumflex humeral artery arises at the lower border of subscapularis, runs backwards with the axillary nerve through the quadrangular space, winds round the surgical neck of the humerus and anastomoses with the anterior circumflex humeral artery.

Anastomosis around the scapula links branches of the first part of the subclavian artery (suprascapular artery and the deep branch of the transverse cervical artery from the thyro-cervical trunk), branches of the third part of the axillary artery (subscapular and circumflex scapular arteries) and the posterior intercostal arteries from the descending thoracic aorta.

Anastomosis around the surgical neck of the humerus (cruciate anastomosis) links the descending branch of the suprascapular artery from the subclavian, the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries from the third part of the axillary, and the ascending branch of the profunda brachii from the brachial artery.

Anastomosis around the shoulder joint links the acromial and deltoid branches of the thoraco-acromial artery, the suprascapular artery from the subclavian and the ascending branch of the anterior circumflex humeral artery.

The axillary vein begins at the lower border of teres major by union of the basilic vein and the two venae comitantes of the brachial artery, ascends on the medial side of the axillary artery, and ends at the outer border of the 1st rib at the apex of the axilla by becoming the subclavian vein; its tributaries correspond to the branches of the axillary artery plus the cephalic vein, the venae comitantes of the brachial artery and the basilic vein.

The axillary lymph nodes are arranged anatomically into five groups related to the walls and apex of the axilla, usually along the blood vessels: anterior (pectoral), posterior (subscapular), lateral (humeral), central and apical.

The anterior (pectoral) group lies along the lower border of pectoralis minor with the lateral thoracic artery, receiving from the central and lateral quadrant of the mammary gland and the anterolateral trunk above the umbilicus, and draining to the central and apical nodes.

The posterior (subscapular) group lies on the posterior axillary wall along the subscapular artery, receiving from the posterior trunk down to the iliac crest and the back of the shoulder region, and draining to the central and apical nodes.

The lateral (humeral) group lies medial and behind the axillary vein in the lateral wall, receiving from the upper limb except the cephalic vein territory, and draining to the central nodes, apical nodes and lower deep cervical nodes.
The central group lies in the fat above the base of the axilla, receiving from all the preceding groups and draining to the apical group.

The apical group lies at the apex of the axilla along the medial side of the axillary vein, receiving from all axillary groups, from the upper and peripheral mammary gland and from the upper limb via the cephalic vein lymphatics, and draining a few efferents to the lower deep cervical nodes and the majority to the subclavian lymph trunk.

Surgically the axillary lymph nodes are divided into three levels relative to pectoralis minor: level 1 below it (anterior, posterior and lateral groups), level 2 deep to it (central group) and level 3 above it (apical group).

keyPoints: The deep fascia of the arm (brachial fascia) forms a sheath for the arm muscles, thin in front and thick behind, and sends two fibrous septa - the lateral and medial intermuscular septa - deeply among the muscles, separating the flexor (anterior) from the extensor (posterior) group and providing additional surfaces for muscle attachment.
The arm is divided by the intermuscular septa into an anterior (flexor) compartment containing three muscles and a posterior (extensor) compartment containing one.

The flexor group consists of biceps and coracobrachialis superficially and brachialis deep to them; they are supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, with the small lateral part of brachialis also supplied by a twig from the radial nerve.

Biceps brachii arises by a short head from the tip of the coracoid process (with coracobrachialis) and a long head from the supraglenoid tubercle whose tendon runs in the bicipital groove; it inserts into the radial tuberosity by the bicipital tendon and into the deep fascia by the bicipital aponeurosis.
Biceps is a powerful supinator when the elbow is flexed, flexes the elbow, its long head tendon stabilises the humeral head and its short head assists shoulder flexion.
Coracobrachialis arises from the tip of the coracoid process, inserts into the midpoint of the medial border of the humeral shaft and assists flexion and adduction of the shoulder joint.

Brachialis arises from the lower half of the anterior humeral shaft and the anterior aspects of the medial and lateral intermuscular septa, inserts into the coronoid process and ulnar tuberosity, and is the primary flexor of the elbow.

Triceps arises by a long head from the infraglenoid tubercle, a lateral head from the upper lip of the spiral groove on the posterior surface of the humerus, and a medial head from the posterior surface of the shaft below the spiral groove.

Triceps inserts into the upper surface of the olecranon process, with a few fibres called articularis cubiti emerging from the deep surface of its lower part to insert into the posterior part of the fibrous capsule of the elbow.

Triceps is supplied by the radial nerve - in the axilla to the long and medial heads and in the spiral groove to the lateral and medial heads; it is the powerful extensor of the elbow joint, and articularis cubiti draws up the posterior part of the elbow capsule during extension preventing it from being caught inside the joint.
The nerves of the arm are the musculocutaneous, radial, ulnar and median.

The musculocutaneous nerve arises in the axilla from the lateral cord, descends lateral to the third part of the axillary artery and the uppermost part of the brachial artery, pierces coracobrachialis, and descends obliquely between biceps and brachialis supplying these three muscles.

About one inch above the elbow the musculocutaneous nerve pierces the deep fascia at the lateral border of the biceps tendon to become the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, dividing into anterior and posterior branches which supply the skin of the lateral side of the forearm and the upper part of the ball of the thumb.
The radial nerve arises in the axilla as the larger terminal branch of the posterior cord, descends on the posterior wall of the axilla behind the third part of the axillary artery.

In the upper arm the radial nerve passes downwards and laterally behind the proximal part of the brachial artery, separating it from the long head of triceps; in the middle it passes between the long and medial heads of triceps into the spiral groove, running downwards and laterally between the lateral and medial heads with the profunda brachii vessels.

In the lower third the radial nerve pierces the lateral intermuscular septum with the radial collateral artery to reach the front of the arm, descending between brachialis and brachioradialis to the front of the lateral epicondyle, where it gives the posterior interosseous nerve (mainly muscular) and continues as the superficial radial nerve (mainly cutaneous).

Radial nerve branches in the axilla: muscular to the long and medial heads of triceps, and the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm supplying the skin on the back of the arm from the deltoid tuberosity down to the elbow.

Radial nerve branches in the spiral groove: muscular to the lateral and medial heads of triceps and anconeus; the lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm supplying skin on the lower lateral surface of the arm; and the posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm supplying skin in the middle of the back of the forearm down to the wrist.

In the lower arm, in the groove between brachialis and brachioradialis, the radial nerve gives muscular branches to brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus and a small lateral part of brachialis.

The brachial artery begins at the lower border of teres major as the continuation of the axillary artery, descends on the medial side of the shaft of the humerus, passes to the front of the arm and descends midway between the epicondyles into the cubital fossa.
It ends in the cubital fossa below the elbow joint at the level of the neck of the radius by dividing into radial and ulnar arteries.

The brachial artery is superficial throughout its course, covered only by skin and superficial and deep fasciae, slightly overlapped by coracobrachialis and the medial edge of biceps, and is accompanied by two venae comitantes.

At the middle of the arm, opposite the insertion of coracobrachialis, the median nerve crosses the brachial artery from lateral to medial, the ulnar nerve leaves it by piercing the medial intermuscular septum into the posterior compartment, and the basilic vein and medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm leave it by piercing the deep fascia to become superficial.

The profunda brachii artery is the largest and highest branch, arising from the posteromedial aspect of the brachial artery just below the lower border of teres major; it accompanies the radial nerve backwards between the long and medial heads of triceps through the lower triangular space to the spiral groove, covered by the lateral head of triceps.

Profunda brachii branches: muscular to triceps, a small nutrient artery to the humerus (may be absent), an ascending branch anastomosing with the descending branch of the posterior circumflex humeral artery in the cruciate anastomosis, and two terminal descending branches - anterior descending (radial collateral) and posterior descending (middle collateral).
The superior ulnar collateral artery arises about the middle of the arm opposite the insertion of coracobrachialis and accompanies the ulnar nerve to the back of the medial epicondyle.

The inferior ulnar collateral artery arises above the elbow joint, gives an anterior branch descending to anastomose with the anterior ulnar recurrent artery in front of the medial epicondyle, then pierces the medial intermuscular septum to reach the back of the medial epicondyle.
Other brachial branches are the nutrient artery to the humerus, muscular branches to biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis, and the terminal radial and ulnar arteries.
The anastomosis around the elbow joint is between the brachial artery above and the radial and ulnar arteries below, described around the medial and lateral epicondyles.

Around the medial epicondyle: behind it, the superior ulnar collateral and the posterior branch of the inferior ulnar collateral meet the posterior ulnar recurrent artery; in front of it, the anterior branch of the inferior ulnar collateral meets the anterior ulnar recurrent artery.

Around the lateral epicondyle: behind it, the posterior descending (middle collateral) branch of profunda brachii meets the posterior interosseous recurrent artery; in front of it, the anterior descending (radial collateral) branch meets the radial recurrent artery.
A transverse anastomosis lies above the olecranon fossa between the inferior ulnar collateral and the posterior descending branch of the profunda brachii.
